The house resumed, from May 1, consideration in committee of Bill No. 19, to amend the Naturalization Act-Mr. Rinfret-Mr. Johnston in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, when
the committee rose I was endeavouring to direct attention to the fact that the submissions we have made to the committee were that under the provisions of the statute in some of the British possessions regulations are made by the governor in council to carry into effect the provisions of the statute, but that in other countries, notably in South Africa, instead of the regulations being made by the governor in council, and subject to being rescinded at will by the governor in council, substantive provisions were introduced into the statute itself.
Last evening the Secretary of State was good enough to suggest that an amendment might be made, which amendment deals only with the question of notice. Now, having conceded the point that the giving of notice should not be done by order in council, I think the Secretary of State must be logical and introduce an amendment to indicate how he is to apprise himself as minister whether or not there has been a compliance by the applicant with the provisions of the statute with respect to residence, character, and adequate knowledge of the English or French language. If it is necessary to add to this bill a provision with respect to the posting of notice in the post office, much more is it necessary that the essential provisions which are standard throughout the empire should in some measure be dealt with in the bill so far as compliance with them is concerned. In other words, since we have now by this amendment sought to provide the means by which notice shall be given to the world, namely, by the

posting in the post office of a notice, which will be torn down the day after it is put up, and which is exactly the thing they refused to do in South Africa and in other communities, where they provide that the notice shall be printed in the Gazette or in a newspaper circulating in the district where the applicant resides-if it is necessary to provide in the bill for the mere posting of the notice in a country post office where it will disappear twenty minutes after it is put up-
Why would it?

Because in these small
country post offices that is the fate of all notices.
No.

Except the notices that
are protected by the statute, by the Post Office Act itself.
No.

The hon. gentleman from Weyburn has had much more experience than I, and therefore I accept his view with respect to the matter. I can only say, having some knowledge of the fate of notices of that character, that they do not continue long in place, and we had a noteworthy example of that when we had a provision in the old electoral act under which the lists were hung up at given points, and they disappeared sometimes twenty-four hours, sometimes thirty-six and sometimes forty-eight hours after being hung up.
The point I make is that we have dealt now with only one feature, namely, the question of notice, and since we have thought it desirable to deal by legislative enactment with the question of notice, much more is it necessary that we should deal in the statute itself with'the method by which the minister is to become apprised whether or not the applicant has met the standard requirements of the act. I asked the minister last evening, I ask him tc-day, and I suppose we will have to continue to ask him, by what means he proposes to make known to himself as minister, in his judicial or executive capacity, whether or not these provisions have been complied with.
Recall, Mr. Chairman, that in the early discussion of this measure the minister desired to have uniformity. That was one of the words he used. He said that judicial discretion had been exercised in different ways throughout Canada, and that now he desired uniformity. Is he to get uniformity from a homestead inspector in Saskatchewan, from

Naturalization Act
a mounted policeman in New Brunswick, and from other agents in other provinces? There are nine provinces in this confederation, nine provinces in which there can be naturalization, and by what method, I ask, through what means, does the minister propose to satisfy himseif, as the high executive official empowered to discharge a very great duty, as was pointed out both by Mr. Churchill and Sir John Simon, with respect to the naturalization of a person within the king's dominions throughout this empire-how does the minister propose to make known to himself whether that parson named John Smith resided in Canada during the period in question? He has answered that question. He has answered it, in my judgment, in accordance with the principles that prevail in the United States. He has stated that he proposes to have those documents transmitted to the Department of Immigration, and to have them indicate whether or not there is a verification in their records of the statements made by the applicant as to the ship on which he arrived, or the train on which he came and where he crossed the border, so that a check up can be made by the department of the allegations made in the application. That is what they do in the United States, only there it is provided by statute that these documents shall be transmitted to the Department cf Trade and Commerce or to the Department of Labour

I think it is both-for the purpose of having the statements verified.
I now come to the second point. How is the minister to satisfy himself that the applicant has an adequate knowledge of the English or French language? That is my difficulty. How is he going to do it? That problem I find engaged the attention of our legislators in the early days, and we concluded, with our limited form of naturalization, that instead of it being done as might have been suggested then in another way, that the responsibility should be placed upon the judges. I do submit to the Secretary of State and to the Prime Minister that this is a very difficult, problem. If we take this responsibility away from the judges-I confess that I have thought of every means suggested by the minister; I have thought it over during the night-I can only point out that inasmuch as uniformity is desired, judicial decisions are the nearest approach that we can get >to it in this country. The minister points out that that is not very good, but that is the nearest approach that we can get to uniformity. What are the reasons urged against it?
The reasons that are urged against it are that it puts the applicant to the inconvenience of travelling a certain distance to meet the 56103-165
judges. I am sorry the Minister of Agriculture is not in his place, but perhaps it is just as well that he is not. When he made light of the whole proceedings last evening, and said that it meant they were going to have a new game called chasing the judge, that was so unworthy of a minister of the crown in dealing with a matter of this kind that in the subsequent observations I made I passed it by. It is degrading to this parliament that the matter should thus be treated, because when the minister spoke of this as a new game of chasing the judge, he knew, as all members know, that there are court houses in which the judges sit, and that there are provided by the provinces buildings for that purpose, and that in the gazettes and newspapers of the provinces there are indicated the days and dates and the places at which the courts will sit. I pointed out, in answer to an interjection by my hon. friend from Yorkton (Mr. M'cPhee) yesterday, that the provincial governments determine where the courts shall sit, and if any inconvenience is being worked by reason of this provision, the provincial government can remedy that overnight. It can provide for a sitting of the district court at any particular point, and as I say, in the province of Alberta does so. I do not know that Alberta is at all exceptional as compared with the other western provinces in that respect, but in the province of Alberta the government. gets the best information it can obtain, and then says that there shall be sittings of the district court at designated small communities, such as Olds, Okotoks and other points that perhaps mean nothing to the hon. gentlemen opposite, but they are the names of the places at which the courts will sit. Therefore the applicant is enabled to know where he will find the judge. He has the right to go to the clerk of the court and ask him; he has the right to go to the process issuer and ask him, and the sittings of the court are as provided, not by this government, for there is no responsibility upon this parliament in respect to the matter-all that this parliament has to do is to provide the judges, and the judges have cast upon them by statute the duty, and that duty they must discharge. That is part of the judicial duties imposed upon them by a statute of the parliament of Canada. The imposition of that judicial duty by statute of this parliament still leaves open to the provincial authorities the determination of the points at which the courts shall sit, and the days on which the courts shall be opened.

As a matter of fact the act as it stands today gives judges discretion in deciding whether or not an applicant is a fit and proper person to be naturalized and if for no other reason than that the act as it now stands gives the judge that discretion, it should be left as it is. We have in the Dominion of Canada at least one judge who is Canadian enough and courageous enough to decline to recommend an oriental as a fit subject for naturalization in this country, and I think the majority of the people will agree with his decision on that point.

Is there in the statute
anything directing the judge to act like that, or is that not rather a matter of policy that should be left to the government to decide?

Section 26 provides :
If the court decides that the alien is a fit and proper person to be naturalized and possesses the required qualifications a certified copy of such decision shall be transmitted by the clerk of the court to the Secretary of State of Canada together with the application and such other papers, documents and reports as may be required by any regulation made hereunder.
The wording is:
If the court decides that the alien is a fit and proper person to be naturalized.
Surely that is as broad a discretion as anyone could have. The judge decides whether the man is a fit and proper person, and the fact that he will never make a proper citizen of this country is sufficient to justify any judge in declining to recommend an oriental for naturalization. They cannot be assimilated into our nationality, and Japan does not extend to us equal privileges in the way of naturalization. The law in Japan requires that an applicant shall, as a consequence of acquiring Japanese nationality, lose his original nationality. Our Naturalization Act does not require anything of that kind. In fact Japanese, notwithstanding the fact that they may go through the form of naturalization in Canada are not released by the Japanese government from their allegiance to Japan. The Japanese government never regard them as aliens; they are still subject and liable to the kingdom of Japan. For that, if for no other reason, we should not change our Naturalization Act. If the evidently inspired despatch from Ottawa expresses the policy of the Secretary of State in regard to naturalization of orientals, there would be no check on them at all. If it is left to the Secretary of State to say whether or not an oriental should be naturalized, his

opinion and that of the department is that a judge has no right to refuse such naturalization. I believe the Canadian people as a whole will say that the judges are right and that orientals are not fit and should not be allowed to be naturalized in this country. They are not assimilable here because they cannot properly and successfully intermarry with Canadians. Is there a member in this house that would like to see his son or his daughter intermarry with an oriental? Certainly not. That means that they are not assimilable; they are not fit and proper persons to be citizens of this country, and probably, no oriental would want to see his children intermarry with ours. That is a feature of the act that is of value to the Dominion of Canada. I will go this far, that if the government will by a definite statutory provision prohibit the naturalization of orientals in this country I for one will be prepared to support the legislation.
I do not think the amendment suggested by the minister improves his bill as originally introduced. It may be that the posting up of notices in post offices will give notice to more people interested in an application for naturalization than the present system of posting the notice in the office of the clerk of the court. If that is so I would say that that requirement should be added to the present one and that the applicant should be required not only to have a notice posted up in the office of the clerk of the court but to have a notice posted up in the post office; but we should not remove any safeguards which the act at present provides.

There is just one phase of the bill now before the house to which I should like to direct the attention of the government. Prior to 1914, naturalization in Canada and in all the other British dominions, in fact in all the possessions of the crown throughout the world, was a matter of purely local jurisdiction. Prior to 1914 in this country application was first made to the clerk of the court. It was supported by affidavit, passed upon pro forma, and a certificate issued to the applicant making him, if you please, a Canadian citizen and entitling him within the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament to the rights and privileges of a Canadian citizen. Prior to that time we had had arising from time to time in Canada a constitutional discussion which is symbolic of the discussions that have occurred since the late imperial conference, and indicative of the class of discussions which are 'bound to arise in the future in regard to a number of subjects which

are within the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament but yet are within the legal legislative juris'dicton of the parliament of Great Britain and also within the legislative jurisdictions of the other dominions, as regards all their citizens and property rights within those dominions.
After the British North America Act was passed providing in section 91, subsection 25 that the parliament of Canada should have legislative jurisdiction with regard to naturalization and aliens, I remember very well that the question then arose of the necessity of preserving the autonomy of Canada in respect of all legislation respecting the naturalization of aliens within the jurisdiction of the Canadian parliament. No doubt after the British North America Act of 1867 was passed, there was the legal right on the part of the imperial parliament, so-called, to legislate that British subjects naturalized under the laws of Great Britain or under the laws of other British dominions should have the rights of British subjects and Canadian citizens within the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. But by conceding to the parliament of. Canada, under the section of the British North America Act which I have just quoted, the exclusive right to legislate with regard to the naturalization of aliens, the parliament of Great Britain, in a constitutional sense, placed it beyond the constitutional right and power of the parliament of Great Britain to legislate upon that subject by the enactment of statutes which would apply within the territorial jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. These discussions proceeded from year to year until the imperial conference of 1911. It was then decided that some way out of the difficulty should be found by mutual agreement between the parliaments of the dominions and the parliament of Great Britain, and that it must be found by such a compromise as would mot impose upon Canada, an autonomous dominion, imperial legislation without the consent of the parliament of Canada.
That compromise was framed by the drafting of the imperial act of 1914. That imperial act for the first time made provision that an alien who had become by naturalization a Canadian citizen might also have the rights and privileges of a British citizen throughout the empire. I remember many instances happening which showed how necessary it was that naturalized aliens should have those rights. I remember the case of a young child of German parentage coming with his parents to British Honduras, receiving his education in the schools of British Honduras, becoming

a member of the legislature of that colony, and subsequently becoming the acting governor of the colony, a man of the utmost probity and ability. He happened to pass across the border into a neighbouring state, and there he was seized upon and placed in gaol, and upon his appeal to the British government for the assistance of British diplomacy, under the circumstances, this man, who had been the representative of the sovereign in his own colony, was refused by the British government the right to ask for their intercession in the premises because, although a British citizen within the territory of British Honduras, he was not a British subject and a British citizen outside of that territory. That and many other similar instances led the imperial conference of 1902 to discuss the matter. Later it was considered at the imperial conference of 1907, and again at the imperial conference of 1911, in which the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier participated. That conference of 1911, while protesting against the proposed legislation as laid before it at that date, under which imperial legislation with respect to naturalization would apply to the dominions, nevertheless agreed-by mutual agreement between the dominions, each legislature in its own behalf insisting upon its own autonomy-that the alien who obtained Canadian citizenship, for instance, within Canada, should have the right of British citizenship throughout the empire. That compromise was embodied in the act of 1914 of the British parliament, which was thereafter adopted by each of the parliaments of the British dominions. So that our autonomy was not interfered with in any way, but these several dominions, by agreement among themselves, by associating together and adopting the same stipulations, agreed, so long as those same conditions might exist, that we in Canada by conferring Canadian naturalization upon any alien would at the same time give to that alien the rights of a British citizen in Australia, the rights of a British citizen in South Africa, the rights of a British citizen in Great Britain and in all her colonies and possessions. Therefore, at the present moment it seems to me that we should not depart in any way, except under absolute necessity, from the agreement which the associated dominions and Great Britain then came to, which was embodied in the imperial act of 1914, and in the bill submitted to this parliament in 1914; because we are now entering upon the consideration of a large sphere of subjects of inter-imperial interest, in which such association and such general agreement must be arrived at in order to ensure the continued association of the dominions, and the maintenance of the rights of citizens of one dominion within the territory of another as well as within Great Britain.
If we were merely legislating to-day with regard to the naturalization of aliens in Canada, certain considerations would apply. It may be necessary, in order that naturalized citizens may have the right to -land titles, perhaps to the franchise and other local privileges, that we should again maintain in a separate classification those who are admitted to Canadian citizenship but who are not admitted to British citizenship throughout the dominions of the empire. But when we amend this act in the form in which the present proposed amendments are brought down we are not only legislating for the admission of aliens domiciled or resident in Canada to the rights of Canadian citizenship within the territorial limits of Canada, but we are legislating. under the reciprocal agreement with Great Britain and the reciprocal legislation passed by the dominions since 1914, to admit those naturalized aliens, domiciled and resident in Canada, into British citizenship, into Australian citizenship, into citizenship in the South African state, into citizenship in Newfoundland and in every other dominion or colony.
If you will look at the statistics you will find that I am within the limit, I think, when I say that the aliens admitted to citizenship in Canada annually aggregate in number about four times the number of aliens admitted to British citizenship throughout all the rest of the British Empire. The reason was explained by one of my hon. friends in the debate of yesterday, that very few aliens go in to take up their residence in Australia, or in South Africa or in New Zealand. But in Canada we are offering very great inducements to immigrants from foreign states. We are putting forth efforts in that direction which are unequalled by all the other British dominions. Therefore it behooves us, I think, to consider not only that we are admitting these aliens as Canadian citizens, but that under a reciprocal arrangement made with the sister dominions and Great Britain we are admitting them to rights and privileges, which are highly prized by many of us, of British citizenship throughout the whole British Empire. Consequently we should proceed with a certain degree of care and circumspection.
It seems to me as the debate proceeded that the difficulties to which the hon. Secretary

of State referred, and which apply almost exclusively to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, might be remedied if the justices of a lower class in those provinces, especially in the remote sections, were permitted to make the examinations and reports now made by the judges of a higher court. I do not know sufficiently the local arrangements in those provinces, but I understand there are district magistrates in almost every remote icom-munity, and if not- there are at least justices of the peace, two of whom might act, and who under the criminal jurisdiction now exercise large powers in those remote districts. While I grant that every opportunity should be given to those residing there to become Canadian citizens^ and British subjects, I think the difficulties mentioned by the Secretary of State might be obviated in the manner I have suggested.
I remember the debate that took place in 1914, because as a student of this matter from early days I took a great interest in those negotiations. In Great Britain the power to refuse a certificate to an applicant for naturalization, which has vested in the Home Secretary since 1844, was exercised, as one hon. gentleman said, for diplomatic purposes. Very few people have been naturalized in Great Britain. From the earliest times up to 1844, when the king in the exercise of his prerogative could accept the allegiance of a foreigner and grant him naturalization, the status of a British subject was regarded as a very high and unusual privilege. In 1844 Great Britain, with that diplomatic subtlety for which she is distinguished, vested in the Home Secretary the absolute right of refusal to grant naturalization, so that the government, without enacting invidious distinctions as between aliens, might through the exercise of this discretion by the Home Secretary, effect its purpose without giving any excuse for its action.
Now, the imperial act of 1914, the framework of which to a large extent was in accordance with the suggestions made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier at the colonial conference of 1911, sought to maintain and preserve the autonomy of this country. This framework was agreed upon in negotiations between Canada, Great Britain and the other dominions, and the form in which it was submitted to this parliament in 1914 reserved to the Secretary of State of Canada the right to refuse naturalization to any alien. But that right was so vested for a particular purpose-so that the government through him might refuse to certain alien races the right to become naturalized Canadian citizens, without making invidious distinctions by statute which might prove irri-
tating to other races in various parts of the world with whom we must preserve at least a certain degree of amity. But that statute of 1914 did provide for a preliminary examination into the qualifications of the applicant by a judge, who decided whether the applicant was a fit and proper person to become a Canadian citizen and a British subject. This removed from a political authority such as the Secretary of State and placed under a judicial tribunal the duty of investigating and the right of deciding whether applications for naturalization should be granted.
I do not wish to go into this at length but if my hon. friends will look at the debates of May, 1914, and particularly at pages 4146, 4179 and 4181, they will find that Sir Wilfrid Laurier made the strongest possible pronouncement against the Secretary of State, under the draft bill then before the house, exercising any discretion whatever in the matter, except that diplomatic discretion which it was deemed necessary to vest in him, in case certain exceptional difficulties arose, to refuse naturalization, and so avoid diplomatic conversations with foreign states. For instance, with regard to the exercise of those powers by the Secretary of State, Sir Wilfrid said:
If a man applies to a judge for a certificate, and a neighbour comes and says that he is not of good character, that he is a fugitive from justice, or has been liable to police punishment, the judge is bound to take cognizance of those matters and refuse the certificate. But wliat we object to is the vesting of such a discretion in a man who is not a judicial officer, but who has political responsibility only. I quite conceive there are many occasions when a discretionary power has to be exercised by the Secretary of State, but the possession of such power is always liable to very serious abuses.
He made an even stronger statement at page 4179. In moving to strike out the clause of the bill of 1914 which gave this discretion to the Secretary of State, the clause which now appears in the act, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
In other words-
After quoting the section.
-you provide machinery for aliens who desire to become citizens, but when the alien passes through that machinery, when he has gone before the judge and has the judge's decision that naturalization should be granted him, the Secretary of State may, without reason given and without possibility of appeal, deny him that privilege. The reasons given for this by the Minister of Justice yesterday do not seem to me to be adequate. I understand him to say that there may be cases in which, for reasons which cannot be told, it may be conducive to the public welfare that a man should not be given naturalization.

Sir Wilfrid goes on to say:
In other words, you re-establish in the hands of the Secretary of State the power which at one time was held by the King of England but which no longer exists. I do not know any justification for that. This section provides that a man must be of good character in order to be naturalized and when he establishes his good character before the judge I do not see why he should not be naturalized.
And then, referring again to the same subject, Sir Wilfrid at page 4181 says, as to the powers of the Secretary of State:
He can do as was done for some time in England before the law of 1844 passed, when naturalization would be granted to some rich Jew, to a foreign prince, or to an important personage from a foreign country. But it will not be King George IV as it was in the days of old-it will be King Louis Coderre-
Referring to the then Secretary of State. -who will grant the naturalization to anybody he pleases. I move that this section be also struck out.
Now, lying at the basis of that whole discussion was the apprehension on the part of Sir Wilfrid that if the entire machinery of investigating applications for naturalization in Canada were placed within the control of the head of a political department it would give rise to the suspicion and the fear that from time to time the political heads would use that power for strictly partisan purposes. If you read these debates you will see that Sir Wilfrid, of all men, insisted that there should be a judicial inquiry. He interpreted the law as it then passed to mean that the procedure enacted by the 1914 act was binding upon the Secretary of State, and that, preliminary to the exercise of any discretion by the Secretary of State, there would be findings and decisions by a judge, after due inquiry in which all parties would be heard. And he felt that that judicial inquiry, to a very considerable extent, withdrew from the political head, the Secretary of State, the exercise of his discretion of admitting all foreigners who claimed qualification under the act. But it did not take from the Secretary of State the power to refuse, for high motives of political policy, the admission of some who may have been qualified under the act,
and who may have been passed by the judge of the court to which application was first made.
Then, in order to remove similar apprehensions to-day, in order that my hon. friends opposite may adhere to the policy so clearly announced by their esteemed leader in past days, it seems to me that they might attain that which they desire to attain, they might remove those difficulties which are now obvious in certain unsettled parts of the provinces of the middle west, by authorizing some minor judicial authority to undertake a judicial inquiry in those remote districts, and at the same time place it, at least apparently, beyond the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State to admit thousands of people wholesale on his mere ipse dixit, and upon an inquiry made by him alone.
There is no difficulty in a city like Montreal. I do not know the statistics, but I venture tire suggestion that in the city of Montreal we admit as many aliens to citizenship within a year-on the average-as are admitted in either of the provinces of the middle west. While I have the greatest confidence in the Secretary of State I should not like, when I am running an election in my own constituency, if ever I should again run an election in St. Lawrence-St. George, to have the Secretary of State, thirty or sixty days before the election, admit a thousand or two persons there, on his own ipse dixit, thus increasing the electoral lists of the St. Lawrence or the St. George subdivisions. A judicial inquiry such as is prescribed gives all confidence to the other dominions that we are living up to the very essence of the agreement which was made between the associated dominions and Great Britain in 1914.

In what other country of
the British Empire is a judicial inquiry insisted upon?

In no other country. In
Canada we have insisted upon it simply because we in Canada are admitting, year by year, to Canadian and British citizenship, four times as many people as are admitted by Great Britain and all the other dominions together. Admissions are very few and exceptional in Great Britain to-day in proportion to its population.

But is it a question of
numbers?

It is a question of numbers, because the fact that 17,000 are admitted on the average each year to Canada-this has

But the judicial inquiry does distribute among the courts of the country the duty and responsibility of investigating applications. Look at the sections of our act which it is proposed to repeal at the present time. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, I think, in the discussions that took place on the subject, regarded them as the safeguard of the system, giving confidence to the people in this country that aliens were not being improperly admitted wholesale. Prior to our act of 1914, the act in the revised statutes of 1906 as amended by the subsequent act of 1907 did not state in such clear and positive terms that the judge of the court should investigate and make a decision. At that time in Canada there was a great deal of dissatisfaction in both political parties with the way in which that act was being administered, and it was then felt that a larger duty should be placed upon the judge. Therefore section 22 of the act of 1914 provides:
An alien desiring to be naturalized shall apply for a decision establishing that he is qualified and fit to be naturalized under the provisions of this act to any judge. . . .
And so on. That placed upon the judge the duty of ascertaining from the evidence before him not only the qualifications under certain sections of the act but the general fitness of the applicant to be naturalized under the provisions of the act. Then section 25 said:
The applicant shall produce to the court such evidence, that he is qualified and fit to be naturalized under the provisions of this act, as the court may require. . . .

cases. I am sure that in many cases these investigations prove most futile. I have been present in court many times, but as far as I remember attention never was called to any special report from the department of the Secretary of State dealing with the matter, as being evidence pertinent to the inquiry which the judge was conducting. That is as far as I go. Of course I know that the Secretary of State receives a copy of these applications but I did not know that in every case he immediately began an inquiry. I am sure that is a new method which perhaps my hon. friend has inaugurated.

Then I undertand the case, and we are not apart at all. Now the minister is changing the w'hole policy, apparently; instead of retaining the exercise of that high discretion as a part of the prerogative right of the crown, he is making himself and his appointees the

The hon. member
for St. Lawrence-St. George has been urging that we in Canada should live up to the agreement made with the other British countries. I do not believe there is anything in the proposed legislation which would tend to violate that agreement. It is now proposed merely to change the method by which we ascertain whether or not a man is qualified for naturalization, and notwithstanding some statements which have been made the hon. gentleman must admit that the method existing in other British dominions is that of investigation by the department of the Secretary of State, so in adopting legislation of this character in reality we are falling in line with the methods used in other British dominions and in the motherland as well.
The hon. member suggests that on account of the differences existing in Canada we should have another method, and I quite agree that possibly this may be so. I believe we should consider these matters on their merits as they apply to Canada, rather than consider conditions which exist with regard to the Hottentots or some other race in another part of the world. In fact, I find it a little difficult to get back to the actual realities in Canada after having listened for forty minutes to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George.
The hon. gentleman has been talking about diplomatic considerations, and has been explaining to us how a man who could qualify under the statute might not be allowed to become naturalized because of matters of high political policy. That might be in accordance with diplomatie practice, but I would rather be inclined to urge that individuals w'ho can qualify under our statutes by all means should be permitted to enjoy the rights which are there provided. I think we have found ourselves in all kinds of trouble through these devious methods of preventing people from getting what they have every right to expect. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has gone back to 1844 and has dealt with the question of how a foreign prince might have bestowed upon him the high privilege of becoming a British subject. I submit that we are a long way from England in 1844.
We are receiving hundreds of thousands of immigrants. We are spending millions of dollars in trying to bring immigrants in. We are offering them inducements to come, in the way of free homesteads. Our regulations, however, provide for naturalization, and I submit we are not keeping faith with those whom we are inviting to come to this country unless we make it possible for them to qualify in order that they may receive free homesteads and in order that they may enter into the full rights of Canadian citizenship.
I quite admit that our naturalization must be safeguarded, but I am firmly convinced that there is more danger of shutting people out from naturalization than there is of admitting too many of them to naturalization. We have definite rules and statutes governing the classes of people who are to be admitted to naturalization. We are not discussing these at the present time; we are discussing merely the most desiraJble method by which such naturalization may be granted. Let us consider the actual situation in respect to these hundreds of thousands of people who are coming to our shores. If we deny them naturalization we postpone for them any opportunity of participating in our common political life. Sometimes there are those in this house who object to what is known in industrial circles as "direct action"; they say that these men ought never to strike. They say that these men who are out of work ought never to parade. If you deny to them the rights of citizenship, if you deny to them the right of endeavouring to bring about desired reforms by means of constitutional action, can you wonder that sometimes they are driven to take unconstitutional action? Surely we must admit that the strongest safeguard we can have in this country-if we believe in democracy at all-is to have the freest participation by all in our common national life, and if we deny to these people who come to our shores-people who are not criminals by any means, people who come from countries which are just as high in the political scale as our own-if we deny to them the right to participate in our national life we are only laying up to ourselves trouble in the years to come. We must not be placed in the position of urging people to come in, of promising certain things when they do come, and then failing to keep faith with them. We do so at our risk.
I am not quite sure whether or not this proposed legislation is for the best, but I do know that the present arrangement is not at all satisfactory. I suppose we should not discuss here some of the questions that do not immediately come up for consideration. The

language question has been already referred to, and with regard to that I should like to say that, while I suppose it is a good thing for us to insist, in a general way, that immigrants should learn English or French, there are a good many people coming here who are well educated, but do not know and have no opportunity to learn English or French and I do not think we should be too rigid about those matters. Take one class of people, the Icelanders; they are years and years ahead of us in political consciousness and political education. For a thousand years they have had democratic political institutions. I know some of the .men who have come to this country in mature life who find it extremely difficult, when placed in remote places in the west, to learn the English language. I think it is a great hardship to prevent such people acquiring citizenship. I had an instance come to my knowledge in this connection, where an elderly Icelandic woman, who is well educated in her own language, has not been able to become naturalized; she is now seventy years of age and yet she is prevented from receiving an old age pension because of lack of naturalization. I think that is a great hardship. She has done much pioneer work in the west. I think it is stupid, if not indeed cruel, to prevent her being naturalized because of some technical requirement.
It has been stated that our practice is uniform, because in every case the judges have to deal with this matter. I would suggest that the lack of uniformity is one of the reasons why some of us would like to see the act changed. Judges have been very arbitrary, in some cases that I have known, in refusing to grant naturalization certificates. They themselves, in my judgment are prejudiced. They have the right to their own opinions, but they are personally very much prejudiced against certain types of foreigners; in some cases it is against orientals, in others it is against Greeks and Italians, and they have absolutely refused to grant naturalization to people >of these nationalities. I cannot think that is a good thing. I number among my own friends people of these nationalities, people who stand just as high in the social scale as people we meet in this parliament. Why should they be refused naturalization because some ignorant judge, and there are some such, or some prejudiced judge, and there are some such, has decided not to admit foreigners? If we ask aliens to come to this country we must be prepared to go through with the undertaking and see that they are incorporated into the life of this country.

It, has been suggested that complaints come only from a few districts. Personally I have comparatively few newly arrived foreigners in my own constituency, but during the last few years I have had the opportunity of lecturing to labour groups pretty much across Canada, and from Glace Bay, Montreal, Toronto, Fort William, Regina, Saskatoon, Calgary, Edmonton, all through the Crowsnest right through to Vancouver, I have had the frequent experience that men of foreign extraction would come to me after my lecture and say, How can we become Canadian citizens? We have been here five, ten or fifteen years but we have no opportunity of becoming Canadian citizens. I have made inquiries in some cases, and it is true that some of these men have had police records; and I have lived long enough among the immigrants to know that it is very easy for a foreigner to acquire a police record. He may have broken a municipal ordinance-and it is very easy for a new arrival to break one of these ordinances -and then he acquires a police record. Or one of them may have taken part in a strike and some charge have been laid against him, and although that took place ten, fifteen or twenty years ago it has been recorded against him and prevents him becoming a Canadian citizen. I have investigated some of these cases and have found that they stand high in the local community; I could produce certificates from reputable citizens of iall classes in the community, that these immigrants are in every way qualified for naturalization, but nothing can be done under the existing arrangements. That means that there is a bitter feeling growing up on the part of thousands of people who otherwise might become good Canadian citizens.
I venture to suggest to the minister an amendment that I think would be desirable if legislation such as he proposes is to be carried. There might be a danger that the Secretary of State might alct in an arbitrary manner, not merely that he might be willing to naturalize thousands of people, as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has suggested, but on the other hand that he might be inclined to deny citizenship to others who have a perfect right to it. Therefore I would suggest that provision should be made in his bill for some sort of a court of appeal. If the Department of the Secretary of State, betaause of an adverse report concerning a man, refuses to grant naturalization, I would say that if the man himself or anyone opposed to the man's naturalization wants to appeal against the decision there should be some place where such an appeal could be

Surely the man ought to have the right to appeal to a commissioner or judge who might be sent out or selected in the district to hold a public hearing. In that way the interests of the public as a whole would be safeguarded. Such an appeal should be granted either when the complaint came from the mian who felt that he was not being given a fair chance or from the community who felt that the department of the Secretary of State had made a mistake.
At the present time investigations are made by the mounted police, and so far as I can see the proposal is that that duty will still be expected of them. Personally I want to enter a protest against that procedure. To a great many people the police are people who come to protect their homes, but to other classes in the community they are officials who miay be coming to cause their arrest. Away out on the plains of Saskatchewan when a policeman appears at the home of a private individual the opinion generally gets abroad that there is something wrong at that home; that the officer is there to investigate; that the settler may be suspected of bootlegging or something of that kind, and people do not like that. Some hon. member says: "No." I know enough about the prairies to' know that is a very common sentiment among certain classes of most reputable people. I believe the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) said that some people had the same feeling about going to the courts. Ordinary people do not go to the courts unless they are forced to go there in connection with some trouble. It may be all very well for lawyers to sit here and say that the courts are the great safeguard of our liberties. The courts are very profitable for them; they enjoy being around the courts, but for many people the courts mean places in which they are mulcted of their hard-earned money. A court means a place where they may get into trouble and which they want to avoid as far as possible.
I would suggest that citizenship is not in the nature of a crime. I hope the time will come 56103-166
when the duty of policemen will not be largely to suppress crime but rather to do everything possible in the interest of the public. When. I see a policeman doing point duty, safeguarding little children as they cross the street. I see exemplified the ideal with regard to a police force which I should like to have generally adopted. But I conceive that is not the ideal most people have to-day with regard to the police and under existing circumstances it would seem to be wise that someone other than a policeman should be used to make these investigations. If a person has a criminal record, by all means have a policeman investigate ; but if there is no criminal record and if Canadian citizenship is a high estate to which the applicant seeks to secure admission, the least we can do is to send to him someone who will not in any way be associated in his mind with crime.
I offer what may seem a very idealistic suggestion, but I have sometimes wondered whether it might not be well to have a little more ceremony connected with the admission ,to citizenship. I have sometimes considered whether we might not add real value to Dominion day if we would arrange that aliens might be admitted to full citizenship, say, on Dominion day, or on some other fixed day when some little ceremonial could be connected with the matter. In that way naturalization would not be granted in a corner after investigation by a policeman as to whether or not the man was guilty of anything, but the new citizen would be made to feel that he was getting something worth while. I am suggesting Dominion day because it is the national holiday. We should say to these 'people: We grant you this Canadian citizenship ; and we might give them some little token in the way of a card or a medal or something of that kind .that would remind them of the occasion.
They receive their papers.
I am not very much in favour myself, of ceremonial, but it is a big thing for an alien to have all the rights of Canadian citizenship.

British citizenship, and while this may seem a little idealistic it might result in a great deal of good especially amongst people who come from countries where ceremonial is very common and where the populace revels in anything that involves a pageant.

Naturalization Act

I would however return to my main contention that the Secretary of State might consider the bringing in of some amendment by [DOT]which an appeal could be made to his department and an investigation held in the locality iwhere the applicant himself or the objectors .to the application might appear to state his or their side of the case.

As one who homesteaded thirty years ago I must differ somewhat from the leader of the Labour party when he says that a mounted policeman is regarded by citizens as a man who is investigating a crime, and that if a policeman visists a home everybody thinks there must be something wrong with that home, or the policeman would not go there.
I spoke particularly about Saskatchewan.

With regard to that libel on Saskatchewan I may say that the police have many times been dispenser's of various forms of relief. They have been very welcome too and no such slur has been cast upon households which they have visited.

During the days of my homesteading in the district in which I laboured we were very glad to see the mounted policeman come along. He was our friend; he would inquire if there was any difficulty and he always helped us out. My purpose however in rising is to make a plea for the alien homesteader. I would not do away with the provision that the man, before he votes, must know the English language; but it is a hardship to an alien, after he is brought into this country, goes on the land, plugs away for five years, builds a house, stable and barns, grubs the roots out of the land and brings it into cultivation, to be told that before he can get his patent or deed for his land he must do something else, he must learn another language. That is not fair. After he has fulfilled his homestead duties you should give him his patent in order that he may be able to carry on. If he has not his deed he cannot mortgage his land, and he cannot come in under the Farm Loans Act. You tie him up, although he has earned and well earned that property. I think this restriction might very well be taken out of the Naturalization Act and put instead into the Elections Act, where you could provide that before a man should be entitled to vote he must be able to read and write one of the two official languages, and that should apply to Canadian settlers as well as to aliens. I have known Canadians many a

time, when I was in business in Ontario, who could not sign a receipt and had to mark a cross. I think the same qualifications for exercising the franchise should apply to Canadians as well as aliens, much more so in the case of the Canadian, who should be better able to read and write the English language than an alien. So I think we might very well consider in this act the granting of naturalization to aliens who have fulfilled their homestead duties and are of good character, and leave the question of being able to read and write the English language to be dealt with in the Elections Act. Then you do away with the discrimination, and you say to the settler, as you ought to do: After you have fulfilled your homestead duties, if you are of good character, we will grant you your patent and naturalization. I know that men who have lived in the frontier districts will endorse this statement, that the first five years are the hardest on the homestead. During the first five years of my life on the homestead I was fully occupied with my homestead duties, and if I had been told that I had not only to live on the homestead and fence and break thirty or forty acres, and have so many cattle, and build a house and barn, but must in addition learn the German language, I would have said: Take back your homestead, because learning a new language would have been harder to me than all the other work, and by the way, we did not say to these aliens when they came here from Hungary or Iceland or Norway: We will grant you a patent after you have finished your homestead duties and made a good citizen of yourself, and in addition you must learn a foreign language. That language qualification was not mentioned when they came here, and it is not fair to bring it up now.

I would like
to answer a remark made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), Mr. Chairman, and then I would ask you to call it six o'clock. The hon. member spoke of the feeling of the people of Saskatchewan towards the mounted police. As one born in that province and having lived there all my life, perhaps I can speak with some authority as to how our people feel about the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, now the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I do not think there is any class of citizen in the whole of Canada that is more looked up to by our western people than the Northwest mounted police ever since they were organized in 1872. When a policeman comes

to their doors, it is never thought by anyone that it is because of some wrong-doing that has been done, but it was the natural thing for these policemen to call at the homes of all the homesteaders in turn, to see if everything was going well with the homesteader, and if everything was not going well it was the duty of the policeman to report accordingly, and see that help was brought, doctors, nurses, and any other assistance that might be required, and that assistance was supplied by the Royal Northwest Mounted Police so far as possible. Therefore, I do not think that anj'body upon the prairies is at all adverse to having one of the riders of the plains come to his door. I have never seen one that objected. On the contrary, the policeman is always welcomed and invited in for a meal, and although the settler has the right to charge the man for a meal, in very few cases is that ever done. The people of Saskatchewan are proud of the Northwest mounted police, and they know that any job they are put at by the Secretary of State or by any department of the government will be looked after, and looked after well, by that splendid body of men.
